Every morning, Marisol climbed the narrow stairs to her grandfather's workshop, where dozens of clocks ticked out of step with one another. As a small child she had found the noise maddening, but now she barely heard it. Her grandfather, bent over a brass gear no larger than a coin, never looked up when she entered. "Hand me the tweezers," he would say, and she would, and that was their entire conversation until noon. Yet she had come to understand that this silence was not coldness. It was the way he welcomed her: by assuming she belonged there. When a customer once asked why such a quiet girl bothered to visit, her grandfather answered without lifting his eyes. "She is the only one who knows when to stay still," he said. Marisol pretended to polish a clock face, but her cheeks burned with pride.
What is the passage mainly about?

["The history of clockmaking in a small town","A girl's growing appreciation of her grandfather's quiet way of showing acceptance","A child's frustration with a noisy workplace","A customer's complaint about a clock repair"]
The passage traces how Marisol comes to see her grandfather's silence as welcome.

Octopuses are masters of disguise, but the mechanism behind their transformations is stranger than most people realize. Beneath an octopus's skin lie thousands of tiny sacs of pigment called chromatophores, each surrounded by muscles. When the animal wants to change color, its brain signals the muscles to stretch the sacs open or squeeze them shut, altering the pattern across its body within a fraction of a second. Remarkably, octopuses appear to be colorblind; their eyes contain only one type of light-sensing cell. Researchers therefore puzzle over how the animal matches its background so well. One hypothesis is that the skin itself contains light-sensitive proteins that detect surroundings directly, allowing the octopus to "see" with its body. Although the idea remains unproven, laboratory studies have shown that isolated patches of skin react when exposed to light, lending the theory some support.

Before the Erie Canal opened in 1825, shipping a ton of goods from Buffalo to New York City cost about one hundred dollars and took weeks of jolting travel by wagon. The canal, a 363-mile waterway dug largely by hand, cut that cost to roughly ten dollars and shortened the trip considerably. Farmers in the Midwest suddenly found that their grain could reach eastern markets profitably, and they planted more. Towns such as Rochester and Syracuse grew rapidly along the route, and New York City surpassed rival ports to become the nation's busiest. Not everyone benefited, however. Translators are often described as invisible, and the best are said to be those whose work readers never notice. Yet this ideal is more contested than it appears. A translator who renders a novel into smooth, natural English may erase the strangeness that made the original distinctive; the foreign rhythms, unfamiliar idioms, and odd turns of phrase are, after all, part of what the author intended. Some contemporary translators therefore deliberately preserve awkwardness, trusting readers to tolerate friction in exchange for authenticity. Critics reply that a translation no one can comfortably read has failed its audience as surely as one that distorts the original. Seventeenth-century Dutch painters turned away from the grand religious and mythological scenes that had dominated European art. Instead, a rising merchant class wanted pictures of their own world: a woman pouring milk, a tavern crowded with card players, a quiet street after rain. Such works were modest in scale, since they were meant to hang in ordinary homes rather than cathedrals. Yet their apparent simplicity is deceptive. Painters labored over the fall of light on a copper pot or the texture of a linen cloth, convinced that attention to the everyday could reveal something enduring. Some scholars read hidden moral lessons into these scenes, such as warnings against idleness or excess. Others argue that the paintings celebrate ordinary life for its own sake. Probably both views contain some truth, for the artists seldom explained themselves.

Ines Calloway never intended to become a famous bookbinder. Born in 1891 to a family of fishmongers in a northern port town, she took a job sweeping floors in a printing shop at fourteen. There she watched the binders stitch pages together and, in the evenings, practiced on scraps of leather the shop would have thrown away. Within a decade her work was sought by collectors, who praised the way her covers seemed to grow out of the books they protected rather than being fastened onto them. Calloway, however, resisted the label of artist. "A binding is a promise that the pages will survive," she wrote in a letter. "If it is beautiful too, that is a bonus." Her insistence on durability over display shaped a generation of craftspeople who followed her.

Scientists once assumed that the sleeping brain simply rests. Experiments with volunteers have since overturned that view. In one study, participants learned a list of word pairs and were then divided into two groups: one slept for eight hours, the other stayed awake. An octopus has no shell and no bones, yet it survives in waters full of hungry predators. Its best defense is camouflage. Special cells in its skin, called chromatophores, can expand or shrink in a fraction of a second. Each cell holds a tiny sac of color, so the octopus can turn from red to brown to nearly white as it moves across a reef. Some octopuses also change the texture of their skin, raising small bumps to look like rough rocks or seaweed. Scientists once believed the animal relied on its eyes to match its surroundings. However, recent studies suggest that the skin itself may sense light, helping the octopus blend in even when parts of its body are hidden from view. If camouflage fails, the octopus can squirt a cloud of dark ink and escape.

Beginning more than two thousand years ago, a network of trade routes known as the Silk Road linked China with the lands around the Mediterranean Sea. Few merchants traveled the entire distance. Instead, goods passed from trader to trader, and each handoff raised the price. Silk, spices, and paper moved westward, while glass, gold, and horses traveled east. When a honeybee finds a rich patch of flowers, she returns to the hive and performs a figure-eight dance on the honeycomb. The straight middle part of the dance, called the waggle run, carries the message. The angle of the run, measured against gravity, tells the other bees which direction to fly relative to the sun. The length of the run indicates distance: the longer the waggle, the farther the flowers. Researchers who first decoded the dance in the 1940s were astonished, because it suggested that insects could share precise information symbolically. Later experiments strengthened that view. When scientists moved a food source while a hive's dancers were advertising its old location, bees that followed the dance arrived at the empty spot and searched there, which showed that they were relying on the dancers' directions rather than simply smelling the food.
What does the length of the waggle run tell other bees?
["How many bees should go","How far away the flowers are","How sweet the nectar is","Which flower is the largest"]
The passage says a longer waggle means farther flowers.

Leaves look green in summer because they contain chlorophyll, a pigment that captures sunlight for making food. As days grow shorter in autumn, trees stop producing chlorophyll, and the green fades. The yellow and orange colors that remain were present all along; they were simply hidden. Red leaves are different. Their color comes from anthocyanins, pigments that many trees manufacture only in autumn, from sugars trapped in the leaves. Bright, sunny days and cool nights produce the richest reds, because sunshine builds up sugar while cold prevents it from leaving the leaf. In a cloudy, warm autumn, the display is usually duller. Brown leaves, finally, result from waste products left behind after the other pigments are gone.
Why do yellow and orange colors appear in autumn?
["They show once the green chlorophyll fades.","Cold air changes green leaves to yellow.","They are produced from trapped sugars.","Trees make them from sunlight in October."]
Those colors were present all along but hidden by chlorophyll.
